# Wastewater can identify where opioid use is high but substance use disorder medications are not well utilized


### Most people who might benefit from taking buprenorphine never start taking it, and of those who start, many don't continue.


[Kait Hess Jimenez, MS](https://substack.com/@kaithessjimenez)


Nov 25, 2026


There are many medications for opioid use disorder meant to ease symptoms of withdrawal and cravings by partially activating the same brain receptors as opioids, while also lowering risk of overdose. Buprenorphine is one such example that can be prescribed in an ordinary primary care office. It sounds too good to be true. For many people it is because most people who might benefit from taking buprenorphine never start taking it, and of those who start, many don’t continue.


New buprenorphine formulations, like extended-release injectables, are trying to address buprenorphine uptake and adherence so that more people can access the care they deserve. However, beyond prescription data, it is difficult to measure if someone continues to take their medication at home or how effective the initial dose is at preventing additional opioid consumption. Wastewater can help in two ways: it shows where opioid use is concentrated, and shines a light on how much buprenorphine is actually in use within a community.


## The treatment gap


In 2022, an estimated 3.7% of U.S. adults, about 9.4 million people, needed treatment for opioid use disorder (OUD). Only 25% of them received medication for it, such as buprenorphine or methadone (


[Dowell et al., MMWR 2024](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/wr/mm7325a1.htm) ). That matches NIDA’s earlier finding that just


[1 in 5 U.S. adults with OUD received medication](https://nida.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/2023/08/only-1-in-5-us-adults-with-opioid-use-disorder-received-medications-to-treat-it-in-2021) in 2021.


To no one’s surprise, the gap is spread unevenly across different demographics. The CDC analysis found that 42.7% of adults who needed treatment didn’t perceive that they needed it, and Black and Hispanic adults were less likely than White adults to receive any OUD treatment.


Starting buprenorphine is a challenge in and of itself, but maintaining treatment is difficult too. A CDC-led study found that unfilled first buprenorphine prescriptions rose from 19% in 2020 to 37% in 2024 (


[Jiang et al., JAMA Network Open 2026](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13439425/) ), though this study excludes those whose prescriptions were filled using medicaid.


Among Medicaid patients who did start, 28% stopped within the first month and 65% within six months (


[Samples et al., J Subst Abuse Treat 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsat.2018.09.001) ). In primary care, fewer than half (44%) stayed adherent over six months, defined as having medication on hand at least 80% of days (


[Hooker et al., BMC Primary Care 2024](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-024-02609-9) ).


Adherence is beneficial not just because of the reduction in overdoses and hospitalizations, but because it reduces the cost burden associated with overall healthcare spending as well (


[Olateju et al., J Subst Use Addict Treat 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.josat.2025.209740) ). Monthly and weekly extended-release injectables were developed largely to close this adherence gap, by removing the patient burden of daily administration.


## Why wastewater


The data the field uses to track treatment, like claims, prescription fills, and national surveys, describe people already in the system, and these data can lag by months to years. In contrast, because wastewater captures everyone connected to a sewer, whether or not they ever see a clinician, Biobot can report results of substance consumption within days of sample collection.


For teams developing and launching buprenorphine products, that opens two uses:


1.


Find the communities with the greatest need: Our opioid and fentanyl data show where use is concentrated, the diversity of substances in use, and where the trend is increasing, which is where focusing treatment and trial sites may matter most.


2.


Track treatment reaching a community over time: Measuring buprenorphine and its metabolite in wastewater gives a population-level read on whether treatment is accessible to those in a catchment and how it correlates with opioid use.


## Finding the communities that need treatment most


Through our national network of over 100 wastewater treatment plant sites, Biobot measures fentanyl and other opioids as well as markers of methadone, buprenorphine, and naloxone. Normalized for population, these data show which communities carry the heaviest opioid burden and how that burden is shifting week to week.


For a development team, that map answers practical questions:


-


Trial site selection: Where are there enough people with OUD to enroll in a study of a new formulation?


-


Launch and access planning: Which high-burden communities have low buprenorphine signal relative to their opioid signal, suggesting an untreated population?


-


Outreach and partnerships: Where should field teams, prescriber education, and community partners be focused first?


FIG. 1: Regional treatment availability relative to opioid use burden. The West has the highest fentanyl use in the country, but buprenorphine observed in wastewater did not scale alongside that increase in opioid use


## Tracking treatment coverage at the community level


When a person takes buprenorphine, it and its main metabolite, norbuprenorphine, reach the sewer. Measured over time and normalized for population, that signal reflects how much buprenorphine a community consumes, including people who never appear in claims data.


On its own, that number can’t tell you whether more people are being treated or the same people are staying in/on treatment, but paired with our opioid data (both of prescription opioids and illicit ones), it becomes a treatment coverage metric: how much buprenorphine a community uses relative to its opioid burden.


That metric opens a few practical comparisons:


-


Coverage gaps: A high opioid signal with a low buprenorphine signal flags communities where need is outpacing access. These are the populations most likely to benefit from new formulations.


-


Change over time: Coverage can be compared before and after a product launch, like a new formulation, a new clinic, or a telehealth program.


-


An open question on injectables: Extended-release injectables release buprenorphine continuously, so growing uptake might produce a steadier community signal.


The natural next step is validation: pairing our wastewater data with a partner’s dispensing data in a few communities to see how closely the two track.


FIG. 2: Norbuprenorphine (buprenorphine metabolite) load relative to norfentanyl over time


## What wastewater can and can’t tell you


Wastewater is a community-level measure. A sample represents thousands to millions of people and carries no personal identifiers, so it can’t tell you who is taking buprenorphine, whether any individual is adherent, or which product they use. Sublingual tablets, films, and injectables all produce the same compounds in wastewater. The signal also includes some buprenorphine used without a prescription, often by people self-treating OUD (


[Han et al., JAMA Network Open 2021](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2785011) ).


What wastewater can do is show population-level trends in near-real-time, something that claims and surveys may miss or report late. It is best complemented with partner data like prescribing, dispensing, and outcomes data, as an early, independent check on whether treatment is reaching the communities that need it.


## Closing the gap


Buprenorphine works when people have access and are consistently utilizing it. New formulations are a big step toward both, but their success depends on reaching the right communities and knowing whether treatment is steady and if their use is decreasing overall opioid consumption.


Wastewater gives developers, payers, and public health partners a fast, privacy-preserving way to see where need is greatest and whether treatment is keeping pace. We’re looking for partners to validate these signals against real-world dispensing data.


Interested in using wastewater data to guide trial design, launch planning, or access programs for opioid use disorder treatment? Reach out to us at hello@biobot.io.
